ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All study procedures were approved by and conducted in compliance with the University of Virginia Institutional Review Board.

N = 104 SGM emerging adults (age: M = 20.21 years, SD = 1.92 years; 76% assigned female at birth; 35% gender minority; 53% Bisexual+; 55% White) were recruited to codesign (Phases 1-2) or complete for 14 days (Phase 3) a daily diary measure of identity-related and non-identity-related stressors and positive identity-related experiences.
In Phase 1, participants completed individual qualitative interviews to provide feedback on a first draft version of the measure that was created by the research team.
table.header: Daily Diary Study of Sexual and Gender Minority Emerging Adults' Stressors: Codesign and Preliminary Findings

table.text: In Phase 3, a larger sample of participants completed the final measure for 14 days.
table.header: Daily Diary Study of Sexual and Gender Minority Emerging Adults' Stressors: Codesign and Preliminary Findings

table.text: We recruited 104 participants (n = 8 in Phase 1, n = 6 in Phase 2, n = 90 in Phase 3) between April 2025 and April 2026.

Participants were recruited via the University of Virginia Psychology Department Participant Pool, digital flyers shared to LGBTQ+-focused email lists, and physical flyers posted in general and LGBTQ+-focused spaces around the University of Virginia and broader Charlottesville, VA community.
Participants were eligible for the study if they were between 18 to 29 years of age, self-identified with a sexual and/or gender minority identity, and owned a smartphone.
Participants were compensated via research credits or digital gift card (1 credit or $20 for Phase 1, 2 credits or $40 for Phase 2, and 4 credits or $80 for Phase 3).
Participants were predominantly college students (79%).
During Phase 1 of the study, n = 8 participants completed a one-hour study visit that included a demographics questionnaire followed by an audio-recorded individual qualitative interview.

Participants were first asked to describe the everyday stressors they experience (including both non-identity-related and identity-related stressors) and how they regulate their emotions in response to these stressors.
Participants were asked about identity-related stressors broadly, not just those related to sexual orientation and gender identity.

Then, participants were given a description of the rationale for the daily diary measure, reviewed the first draft measure that was created by the research team, and were asked to provide feedback on how to improve the measure (e.g., how language or response options should be changed to best capture their experiences).
Finally, participants completed a 30-minute audio-recorded individual qualitative interview and provided feedback on how to improve the measure.
One Phase 2 participant was lost to follow-up, so only n = 5 Phase 2 participants completed a qualitative interview.

During the visit, participants were given additional context by the researcher for several measure items (e.g., clarification that they can consider both acute and chronic stressors; see Supplement Section F for more detail).

During this review, the graduate students noted all potential changes to the daily diary measure and study methods that participants had suggested directly (e.g., participant specifically recommending a change) or indirectly (e.g., participant mentioning a certain item was confusing, or discussing aspects of their experience that were not yet captured by the questionnaire).
table.header: Refining the Measure After Phases 1 and 2

table.text: Specifically, participants completed an average of 84.4% of surveys and took an average of about seven minutes to complete each survey, suggesting the measure yields good compliance and is brief.

The finding that participants had an identity-related stressor on 43.0% of study days is consistent with a prior study of sexual minority adolescents (age 12 to 18 years), which found participants experienced an identity-related stressor on 40.2% of study days (Mereish et al., 2021; though notably their measure captured just distal stressors, whereas ours captured distal and proximal stressors).

table.text: For example, our sample had a higher percentage of college students than SGM emerging adults as a whole, participants were all residents of the same city in the southeastern U.S. (which is relevant given prior research finding different levels of minority stress by geographic region; Pachankis et al., 2021), and certain racial/ethnic groups (e.g., Black SGM emerging adults) were not represented in Phases 1 and 2.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Emerging adulthood involves impactful developmental milestones for sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals and is a critical period for understanding stress processes.
Most existing SGM stress research is cross-sectional, with relatively little known about the everyday experiences that may confer mental health risk or resilience for SGM emerging adults.

N = 104 SGM emerging adults (age: M = 20.21 years, SD = 1.92 years; 76% assigned female at birth; 35% gender minority; 53% Bisexual+; 55% White) were recruited to codesign (Phases 1-2) or complete for 14 days (Phase 3) a daily diary measure of identity-related and non-identity-related stressors and positive identity-related experiences.
Phase 1 participants (n = 8) completed qualitative interviews and provided feedback on an initial draft measure.
Phase 2 participants (n = 6) piloted a revised measure for seven days before providing feedback in qualitative interviews.
Phase 3 participants (n = 90) completed the final measure for 14 days.
Qualitative data from Phases 1-2 were analyzed using the immersion-crystallization framework, and descriptive statistics were computed for Phase 3 quantitative data.

In Phases 1-2, participants emphasized the need to capture chronic stressors and stress tied to recent sociopolitical events in the U.S. In Phase 3, non-identity-related stressors were more frequent than identity-related stressors, proximal identity-related stressors were more frequent than distal identity-related stressors, and negative intersectional experiences and positive identity-related experiences were both common.
Results highlight the importance of involving participants with lived experiences in all stages of survey design.
Sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals experience mental health problems at higher rates than their cisgender, heterosexual peers (Dhejne et al., 2016; Wittgens et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals experience mental health problems at higher rates than their cisgender, heterosexual peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dhejne et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Wittgens et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Minority stress theory is the leading framework through which researchers understand these disparities.

The theory posits that, in addition to the general life stressors experienced by everyone, SGM individuals face additional unique stressors related to the stigmatization of SGM identities, the cumulative stress of which is thought to confer higher risk for mental health problems (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: The theory posits that, in addition to the general life stressors experienced by everyone, SGM individuals face additional unique stressors related to the stigmatization of SGM identities, the cumulative stress of which is thought to confer higher risk for mental health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Minority stress theory distinguishes distal minority stressors (i.e., stigma-related processes originating externally, such as discrimination and microaggressions) from proximal minority stressors (i.e., stigma-related processes activated internally and arising from socialization, such as internalized stigma, expectations of rejection, and SGM identity concealment; Frost & Meyer, 2023).
text.formatted: Minority stress theory distinguishes distal minority stressors (i.e., stigma-related processes originating externally, such as discrimination and microaggressions) from proximal minority stressors (i.e., stigma-related processes activated internally and arising from socialization, such as internalized stigma, expectations of rejection, and SGM identity concealment; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Frost & Meyer, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Recent theoretical and empirical work has extended minority stress theory by acknowledging stress associated with negative intersectional experiences (e.g., perceived conflict between an SGM identity and another identity) as a contributor to mental health problems among SGM individuals who hold multiple marginalized identities (Jackson et al., 2020; Rivas-Koehl et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Recent theoretical and empirical work has extended minority stress theory by acknowledging stress associated with negative intersectional experiences (e.g., perceived conflict between an SGM identity and another identity) as a contributor to mental health problems among SGM individuals who hold multiple marginalized identities <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Jackson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Rivas-Koehl et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, recent work has emphasized positive identity-related experiences as influencing mental health by enhancing positive affect and potentially buffering the deleterious impacts of identity-related stress (Clark et al., 2025; Dyar, Curtis, et al., 2024; Flynn et al., 2026; Mohr & Sarno, 2016; Perrin et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Additionally, recent work has emphasized positive identity-related experiences as influencing mental health by enhancing positive affect and potentially buffering the deleterious impacts of identity-related stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Clark et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Dyar, Curtis, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Flynn et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Mohr & Sarno, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Perrin et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Given the important roles of general life stressors, stressors related to the stigmatization of marginalized identities, negative intersectional experiences, and positive identity-related experiences in contributing to mental health in SGM populations, the current study co-designed and pilot tested a novel measure of these experiences in daily life.
Emerging adulthood (ages 18-29; Arnett et al., 2014) is a developmental period characterized by unique stressors and opportunities for SGM individuals (Wagaman et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Emerging adulthood (ages 18-29; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Arnett et al., 2014)</ref> is a developmental period characterized by unique stressors and opportunities for SGM individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Wagaman et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Gender and sexual identity continue to develop during emerging adulthood (Scroggs & Vennum, 2021), and many people first identify as LGBTQ+ and connect with LGBTQ+ community during this period (Schmitz & Tyler, 2018).
text.formatted: Gender and sexual identity continue to develop during emerging adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Scroggs & Vennum, 2021)</ref>, and many people first identify as LGBTQ+ and connect with LGBTQ+ community during this period <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Schmitz & Tyler, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Many SGM individuals move away from their hometown during emerging adulthood and must navigate when and with whom to disclose their SGM identities in new contexts (Garvey et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Many SGM individuals move away from their hometown during emerging adulthood and must navigate when and with whom to disclose their SGM identities in new contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Garvey et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging adulthood is also often a time in which individuals first explore romantic and sexual relationships (Gala & Kapadia, 2013), which may mean navigating, or at least anticipating, the potential social consequences of being in a visibly queer relationship for the first time.
text.formatted: Emerging adulthood is also often a time in which individuals first explore romantic and sexual relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gala & Kapadia, 2013)</ref>, which may mean navigating, or at least anticipating, the potential social consequences of being in a visibly queer relationship for the first time.

text.text: Many gender minority individuals first become eligible for gender-affirming medical interventions during emerging adulthood (Dai et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Many gender minority individuals first become eligible for gender-affirming medical interventions during emerging adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dai et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, recent increases in legislation and sociopolitical discourse that threaten the rights of SGM emerging adults have had a major impact on LGBTQ+ individuals in this age group (Lee et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Lastly, recent increases in legislation and sociopolitical discourse that threaten the rights of SGM emerging adults have had a major impact on LGBTQ+ individuals in this age group <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lee et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging adulthood is therefore a unique period of identity development, opportunity, and stress for SGM individuals, so it is important to understand the daily experiences of
LGBTQ+ individuals during this unique developmental stage.

Hundreds of prior studies have empirically tested components of minority stress theory and its extensions among SGM individuals in emerging adulthood and other developmental stages, effectively documenting the myriad mental health correlates of minority stress, such as higher negative affect, lower positive affect, and higher internalizing psychopathology (Hoy-Ellis, 2023; Nicholas & Bresin, 2024).
text.formatted: Hundreds of prior studies have empirically tested components of minority stress theory and its extensions among SGM individuals in emerging adulthood and other developmental stages, effectively documenting the myriad mental health correlates of minority stress, such as higher negative affect, lower positive affect, and higher internalizing psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hoy-Ellis, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Nicholas & Bresin, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, the majority of existing empirical research on SGM populations-91% by a recent estimate-is cross-sectional (Walch et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, the majority of existing empirical research on SGM populations-91% by a recent estimate-is cross-sectional <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Walch et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Given the limitations of cross-sectional research (e.g., retrospective bias, inability to separate within-person and between-person effects; Hamaker, 2024; Schwarz, 2007), researchers are increasingly using experience sampling methods (ESM), which are designed to capture psychological processes as they occur real-time in everyday-life situations (Csikszentmihalyi & Larson, 1987), to study SGM stress processes (Nicholas & Bresin, 2024).
text.formatted: Given the limitations of cross-sectional research (e.g., retrospective bias, inability to separate within-person and between-person effects; <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hamaker, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Schwarz, 2007)</ref>, researchers are increasingly using experience sampling methods (ESM), which are designed to capture psychological processes as they occur real-time in everyday-life situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Csikszentmihalyi & Larson, 1987)</ref>, to study SGM stress processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Nicholas & Bresin, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, using ESMs, such as daily diary surveys, to study SGM mental health is still a nascent field, so gaps remain in our understanding of how mental health-related processes unfold in SGM emerging adults' daily lives.

Many of the prior SGM mental health studies leveraging ESM have focused on capturing which identity-related stressors individuals experience on a day-to-day basis, revealing initial insights into the types and frequencies of identity-related stressors SGM emerging adults may face.

To highlight a few examples, one study found that sexual minority adolescent participants experienced at least one distal identity-related stressor on 40% of study days, with seeing or hearing negative messages about individuals with the same identity being the most frequently endorsed (Mereish et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To highlight a few examples, one study found that sexual minority adolescent participants experienced at least one distal identity-related stressor on 40% of study days, with seeing or hearing negative messages about individuals with the same identity being the most frequently endorsed <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mereish et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a study of gender minority emerging adults found that participants experienced stress related to their gender minority identity approximately 10 out of 21 study days, though the authors did not report the relative frequencies of types of identityrelated stressors endorsed (Dermody et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, a study of gender minority emerging adults found that participants experienced stress related to their gender minority identity approximately 10 out of 21 study days, though the authors did not report the relative frequencies of types of identityrelated stressors endorsed <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dermody et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another study of sexual and gender minority adolescents asked participants to write about their identity-related stressors each day and found that participants reported an identity-related stressor on 42.1% of days, with a variety of stressor themes described (e.g., social rejection, identity disclosure, negative representation, etc.) (Sullivan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Another study of sexual and gender minority adolescents asked participants to write about their identity-related stressors each day and found that participants reported an identity-related stressor on 42.1% of days, with a variety of stressor themes described (e.g., social rejection, identity disclosure, negative representation, etc.) <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Sullivan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, looking at one specific type of identity-related stressor, a study of Black sexual minority adults found that participants endorsed negative intersectional experiences (specifically, distal stressors that simultaneously engaged a participants' racial and sexual orientation identities) on 11.4% of study days (Jackson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Finally, looking at one specific type of identity-related stressor, a study of Black sexual minority adults found that participants endorsed negative intersectional experiences (specifically, distal stressors that simultaneously engaged a participants' racial and sexual orientation identities) on 11.4% of study days <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Jackson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Prior research therefore suggests SGM emerging adults may experience an identity-related stressor on roughly one quarter to one half of days (depending on the sample and measurement approach), and that individuals experience a range of specific types of identity-related stressors, including negative intersectional experiences.

However, no prior work to our knowledge has investigated the affective impact of identity-related stressors compared to all the other non-identity-related stressors (e.g., school, work, and social experiences) that define emerging adulthood and contribute to risk for psychopathology (Ringwald et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, no prior work to our knowledge has investigated the affective impact of identity-related stressors compared to all the other non-identity-related stressors (e.g., school, work, and social experiences) that define emerging adulthood and contribute to risk for psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Ringwald et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further, little is known about the contexts in which daily stressors occur, such as how often they are happening online versus offline, and how often they involve other people versus occurring alone.

Understanding which daily stressors are most impactful, and contextual features of these stressors, is necessary to develop effective, adaptive interventions that can support SGM emerging adults when these various stressors occur (i.e., just-in-time adaptive interventions; Nahum-Shani et al., 2018).

text.text: Given no existing measure captured the full range of identity-related and non-identityrelated daily stressors experienced by SGM emerging adults, the present study solicited feedback from SGM emerging adults to iteratively co-develop the Sexual and Gender Minority Daily Experiences Measure (SGM-DEM).
1 After developing the measure, we then tested it in a 14-day daily diary study.
The study comprised three phases.
In Phase 1, participants completed individual qualitative interviews to provide feedback on a first draft version of the measure that was created by the research team.

2 In Phase 2, a separate sample of participants piloted a revised 1 Note that our measure captures several domains similar to measure that was published by Clark and colleagues while data collection for the present study was in progress (2025).
Whereas their measure focuses on stressors tied to SGM identities, our measure is designed to additionally capture intersectional stressors.
2 Multiple members of the research team are themselves sexual or gender minority emerging adults.
version of the measure on their smartphone for seven days before providing feedback in individual qualitative interviews.
"Immersion-crystallization" was used to identify themes in the data and revise the measure after the first two phases.
In Phase 3, a larger sample of participants completed the final measure for 14 days.

In the remainder of this paper, we: 1) describe our approach to iteratively co-developing the measure with participants, 2) highlight participants' qualitative feedback provided during interviews, 3) provide descriptive statistics from the deployment of the final measure with the large sample, and 4) discuss implications of our findings for future research on SGM individuals' daily experiences, and the field of SGM mental health more broadly.
We recruited 104 participants (n = 8 in Phase 1, n = 6 in Phase 2, n = 90 in Phase 3) between April 2025 and April 2026.

Participants were recruited via the University of Virginia Psychology Department Participant Pool, digital flyers shared to LGBTQ+-focused email lists, and physical flyers posted in general and LGBTQ+-focused spaces around the University of Virginia and broader Charlottesville, VA community.
Participants were eligible for the study if they were between 18 to 29 years of age, self-identified with a sexual and/or gender minority identity, and owned a smartphone.
The informed consent process was conducted with a researcher prior to the start of study procedures.
Participants were compensated via research credits or digital gift card (1 credit or $20 for Phase 1, 2 credits or $40 for Phase 2, and 4 credits or $80 for Phase 3).
In Phase 3, credits/payment were prorated based on the percentage of surveys completed.
Among those who participated for payment, the five participants with the highest daily diary completion percentage received a $10 bonus.
The full sample was 76% assigned female at birth, 53% Bisexual+ (i.e., identified as Bisexual or Pansexual), 35% gender minority, 55% White, and the mean age was 20.21 years (SD = 1.92 years).
Participants were predominantly college students (79%).
See Table 1 for detailed demographic information broken down by study phase.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for detailed demographic information broken down by study phase.

text.text: All study procedures were approved by and conducted in compliance with the University of Virginia Institutional Review Board.
Study visits were conducted in person or via Zoom video call, depending on participant preference and researcher availability.
During Phase 1 of the study, n = 8 participants completed a one-hour study visit that included a demographics questionnaire followed by an audio-recorded individual qualitative interview.

Participants were first asked to describe the everyday stressors they experience (including both non-identity-related and identity-related stressors) and how they regulate their emotions in response to these stressors.
Participants were asked about identity-related stressors broadly, not just those related to sexual orientation and gender identity.

This allowed for discussion of stressors related to other identities (e.g., race, ethnicity, body size, disability status, religion, socioeconomic status, etc.) and intersectionality (e.g., stressors related to specific combinations of identities).

Then, participants were given a description of the rationale for the daily diary measure, reviewed the first draft measure that was created by the research team, and were asked to provide feedback on how to improve the measure (e.g., how language or response options should be changed to best capture their experiences).
See Supplement Section A for the interview guide used in Phase 1.

During Phase 2, a separate sample of n = 6 participants first completed a 30-minute initial study visit that involved completing a demographic questionnaire and downloading the RealLife Exp application (an experience sampling platform; LifeData, 2026) on their personal smartphone.
Then, participants went about their lives for seven days while completing the daily diary measure each evening via the RealLife Exp application.
Finally, participants completed a 30-minute audio-recorded individual qualitative interview and provided feedback on how to improve the measure.
See Supplement Section B for the interview guide used in Phase 2.
One Phase 2 participant was lost to follow-up, so only n = 5 Phase 2 participants completed a qualitative interview.

During Phase 3, a third sample of n = 90 participants first completed a one-hour study visit that involved completing a demographic questionnaire, completing several other baseline questionnaires (not analyzed in the present study), downloading the RealLife Exp application on their personal smartphone, and getting oriented to the smartwatch that recorded passive data (also not relevant to the present study) during the subsequent assessment period.

During the visit, participants were given additional context by the researcher for several measure items (e.g., clarification that they can consider both acute and chronic stressors; see Supplement Section F for more detail).
Then, participants went about their lives for 14 days while completing the daily diary measure each evening.
In this phase, study staff followed up over email or phone every other day if surveys were missed to encourage survey completion and offer technical support.

The demographic self-report questionnaire assessed age, sex assigned at birth, gender identity, sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, first language, occupation, disability status, and estimated household income.
Prior to the start of the study, the research team created an initial draft of the daily diary measure to be reviewed by participants in Phase 1.

The measure was designed to capture several content areas relevant to psychopathology risk in SGM emerging adults: 1) Day-level positive and negative affect, 2) the two most intense stressors experienced that day, 3) the emotion regulation strategies participants used in response to these two most intense stressors,foot_0 3) identity-related stressors experienced that day, and 4) positive identity-related experiences.
text.formatted: The measure was designed to capture several content areas relevant to psychopathology risk in SGM emerging adults: 1) Day-level positive and negative affect, 2) the two most intense stressors experienced that day, 3) the emotion regulation strategies participants used in response to these two most intense stressors,<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> 3) identity-related stressors experienced that day, and 4) positive identity-related experiences.

text.text: We designed the measure to be modular, such that future researchers can choose to administer the sections relevant to their research questions.
The initial draft measure used in Phase 1 is presented in Supplement Section C. Several existing measures informed the initial daily diary measure.
Day-level positive and negative affect were captured with the Internationally Reliable Short-Form of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (I-PANAS-SF; Thompson, 2007).
text.formatted: Day-level positive and negative affect were captured with the Internationally Reliable Short-Form of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (I-PANAS-SF; <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Thompson, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: No changes were made to these items during the study to retain the psychometric properties of the I-PANAS-SF.

The two most intense daily stressors were captured via participant free response, and the first-draft follow-up questions about contextual features of these stressors (e.g., domain of stressor) were based partly on our prior research on anxiety-related stressors among university members (Leventhal et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The two most intense daily stressors were captured via participant free response, and the first-draft follow-up questions about contextual features of these stressors (e.g., domain of stressor) were based partly on our prior research on anxiety-related stressors among university members <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Leventhal et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The first draft of the list of emotion regulation strategies that participants could endorse using in response to the two most intense daily stressors was based on our team's prior experience sampling research on emotion regulation strategy use in the daily lives of socially anxious college students (e.g., Daniel et al., 2020 Daniel et al., , 2023)).

text.text: The first draft list of identity-related stressors from which participants could select was adapted from the Everyday Identity Stress Scale (Mereish et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The first draft list of identity-related stressors from which participants could select was adapted from the Everyday Identity Stress Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mereish et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the first draft of positive identity-related experience items were created by the study team.
Our data collection and analysis approach during Phases 1 and 2 was based on the "immersion-crystallization" framework.

Immersion-crystallization is a rapid, iterative, inductive analysis process whose core elements, as the name implies, include immersion (reviewing the data in depth, such as through research team members individually reading and listening to transcripts) and crystallization (reflecting on the analysis experience to identify and articulate patterns or themes noticed during the immersion process, such as through discussion among the research team; Borkan, 2022).
text.formatted: Immersion-crystallization is a rapid, iterative, inductive analysis process whose core elements, as the name implies, include immersion (reviewing the data in depth, such as through research team members individually reading and listening to transcripts) and crystallization (reflecting on the analysis experience to identify and articulate patterns or themes noticed during the immersion process, such as through discussion among the research team; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Borkan, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A key difference from other qualitative research approaches, such as thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), is that immersion-crystallization does not typically generate themes via systematic coding, but rather through a holistic review of the data and researchers' insight.
text.formatted: A key difference from other qualitative research approaches, such as thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Braun & Clarke, 2006)</ref>, is that immersion-crystallization does not typically generate themes via systematic coding, but rather through a holistic review of the data and researchers' insight.

text.text: It therefore tends to be a faster approach, which aligned with our goal to develop and rapidly iteratively refine a measure for use in a large data collection.
Four trained undergraduate research assistants conducted the qualitative interviews, which were then transcribed to text.

Then, following each study phase, a team of four clinical psychology graduate students independently reviewed the transcripts, such that each transcript was reviewed by two individuals (i.e., the immersion step).

During this review, the graduate students noted all potential changes to the daily diary measure and study methods that participants had suggested directly (e.g., participant specifically recommending a change) or indirectly (e.g., participant mentioning a certain item was confusing, or discussing aspects of their experience that were not yet captured by the questionnaire).

Next, the research assistants who led the interviews and the graduate students met as a team to discuss interpretations of the data until consensus was reached regarding how to change the daily diary measure to incorporate participant feedback (i.e., the crystallization step).
Additionally, following Phase 2 of the study, participants' daily diary measure data from Phase 2 were discussed among the research team to further guide measure design.

Specifically, the team checked how long the survey took to complete, how often a top two daily stressor was identity-related, and the frequency with which all identity-related stressors that day were endorsed to check whether the overall measurement approach (i.e., capturing all stressors that day but focusing primarily on the two most stressful experiences) sufficiently captured a range of stressors.
The final version of the measure is presented in Supplement Section E. Researchers interested in using the measure are encouraged to use the final version.
Tables 2 3contain descriptive statistics corresponding to each non-free-response item in the final measure.
text.formatted: Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> <ref type="table">3</ref>contain descriptive statistics corresponding to each non-free-response item in the final measure.

text.text: The final measure first asks about daily affect, then asks about contextual features of the first and second most stressful daily experiences (e.g., the domain of the stressor; whether it was identity related; if identity related, which from a list identity-related stressors best describes what happened; etc.).

It ends with questions about the day as a whole, including presenting participants with checklists to select all identity-related stressors and positive identity-related experiences that occurred that day.

To understand overall endorsement rates for categorical items (i.e., multiple choice and select-all-that-apply questions), we computed the total number of times and percentage of times each response option was selected across the entire sample.
Note that for single-select items, percentages add up to 100%, and for select-all-that-apply items, percentages add up to greater than 100%.

Additionally, to understand endorsement rates at the participant level, we computed the number of participants and percentage of participants who selected each response option at least once during the 14-day study.
For numeric items (i.e., Likert scale, sliding scale, and numeric free-response questions), we computed the means and standard deviations across the entire sample.
In the Results section, we highlight the median (rather than mean) when the distribution of a numeric variable was highly skewed.
Below, we summarize major themes from the qualitative data (from both Phase 1 and Phase 2) that informed design decisions for the study measure.
For clarity, filler words (e.g., "um") are occasionally removed from participants' quotes.
Gender neutral pronouns (i.e., they/them/theirs) are used in this section to limit potential identifiability.
Finally, many participants recommended slight wording adjustments to daily diary measure items.
We typically made these changes, but this more superficial qualitative feedback is not detailed here.
Additional quotes illustrating the qualitative themes are presented in Supplement Section G.
Several participants reported that recent sociopolitical events were significant daily stressors.

For example, one participant discussed how changes in federal and local policy had affected their access to healthcare: "…with all the stuff going on with, like, the administration, that's been a little stressful, because everything got a lot more expensive, and I can't get my testosterone through [the student health clinic] anymore." -P 103
Similarly, in the daily diary free-response question asking participants to describe the most stressful experience that day, several Phase 2 participants wrote about sociopolitical events.
For example, on one day, one participant wrote: "I learned that the Supreme Court ruled today that states can ban gender affirming care for minors." -P 201
Several participants described being impacted by chronic stressors that the initial versions of the daily diary measure did not capture well.
For example, one participant noted, "This survey is only asking about... daily stress.
Sometimes stress, often it's actually... over a long period of time.
It's significantly stressful even though on any given day it's not the most stressful thing that happened." -P 201

Another participant discussed chronic stigma-related stress that they felt was not well captured in early versions of the measure: "That subtle dehumanization that you encounter every single day can build up in a way that gets really exhausting, even if there isn't necessarily one instance one day that, you know, really cements it." -P 205
Several participants discussed identity-related stressors that were not included in initial versions of the measure.

For example, one participant talked about stress tied to uncertainty around their sexual orientation, describing experiencing: "... a lot of questioning my own identity and asking, is this… imposter syndrome where it's like, are you actually gay right now?

Or, is this you saying that you're gay, [but] you're not really gay…" -P 104 Additionally, participants brought up stressors related to social identities not included in early versions of the measure.
text.formatted: Or, is this you saying that you're gay, <ref type="bibr">[but]</ref> you're not really gay…" -P 104 Additionally, participants brought up stressors related to social identities not included in early versions of the measure.

text.text: For example, one participant, a second-generation immigrant, talked about negative rhetoric about immigrants they were seeing in the news: "I feel like there's a lot of negative connotation about the way [President Trump is] talking about the people who are coming here, like them stealing jobs and being in gangs and distributing drugs." -P 105

text.text: Participants described a variety of positive experiences related to their identity that were not captured in initial versions of the measure.
For example, one participant discussed having spontaneous, positive thoughts and emotions related to their sexual and gender identities:

Consistent with minority stress theory (Meyer, 2003; Testa et al., 2017), early versions of the measure differentiated between distal/external stressors (e.g., discrimination) and proximal/internal stressors (e.g., internalized negative attitudes).

text.text: However, several participants reported instances where, in practice, this distinction was difficult to make.
For example, one participant noted: "The first couple of days I had... trouble deciding which of these events is external?
Which of these was internal?" -P 202
Another participant discussed a specific example where they were made to feel uncomfortable by another person and were unsure how to categorize the experience in the measure: "External events...
I don't know, because there's no solid line between internal and external events...
I was made to feel uncomfortable...that's external stimuli, but in an internal feeling." -P 201
Participants discussed engaging in emotion regulation strategies that were not captured well by early versions of the daily diary measure.

For example, early versions of the measure included an option for expressing emotions to other people, but one participant explained that there are times they let out difficult emotions by themselves: "I feel like for some of these it's… expressing your emotions, like getting them out physically, like a physical reaction.
So, sometimes that's like crying, screaming… I feel like that's a fairly common experience.
But, I don't think if I was doing that, I would know where to categorize that under." -P 104

Another participant recommended we add an option explicitly capturing engagement in hobbies: "You could add something about hobbies… Because maybe someone doesn't do any of these [other listed] things, but there's like other hobbies." -P 107
Phase 3 Measure Completion Phase 3 participants combined completed 1,064 out of 1,260 possible surveys (84.4% overall completion rate) over the 14-day assessment period.
An additional 32 surveys were initiated but discontinued prior to completion.
The total number of surveys out of 14 (reflecting one assigned per day) completed by a given participant ranged from one to 14, with a mean of 11.82 (SD = 2.32).
The survey took participants a median time of 6.85 minutes (SD after removing outliers greater than or equal to 60 min = 6.69 minutes) to complete.
In this section, we highlight descriptive statistics for items related to daily affect, stressors, and positive identity-related experiences, from the final measure deployment in Phase 3.
For the full reporting of descriptive statistics, refer to Tables 2 and 3.

text.text: The I-PANAS-SF items showed acceptable internal consistency within and between participants for both positive affect items (ω-within = 0.73, ω-between = 0.89) and negative affect items (ω-within = 0.69, ω-between = 0.92).

Participants most frequently reported that their first-and second-most stressful daily experiences (termed top two stressors below, for brevity) were in the domains of academics, work, or career development (47.5% of stressors), social situations (25.2%), and family and home life (13.5%).

When asked whether a top two stressor was related to an identity they hold, or discrimination or stigma towards an identity they hold, participants most frequently responded "no" (84.6% of stressors) followed by "yes" (10.0%) and maybe (5.4%).
"No" was selected at least once during the 14 days by all 90 participants, "yes" by 60 participants (66.7%), and "maybe" by 46 participants (51.1%).

When a top two stressor was identity-related or maybeidentity-related, participants most often reported that the stressor was related to a sexual minority identity (59.6% of stressors), followed by gender minority identity (29.5%), identity as a woman or man (22.9%), cognitive/psychological disability (12.7%), race (5.7%), or ethnicity (5.7%).
Participants reported that an identity-related top two stressor was related to a single identity for 65.1% of stressors, and multiple identities for 34.9% of stressors.

When asked for the categorical description(s) that led them to endorse an identity-related or maybe-identity-related top two stressor, participants most often selected, "My identity interfered with my life" (31.6%), followed by, "I worried that others would reject or not accept me due to my identity" (25.9%), "I actively concealed my identity from others" (16.9%), and "I felt negatively about my identity or people with my identity," (16.0%).
Participants reported that top two daily stressors involved other people (vs. involving no other people) about half the time (50.8%).
Top two stressors most often occurred offline (86.2%) vs. online.

When asked to report all daily identity-related stressors (not just those among the top two most stressful experiences that day), participants reported experiencing one or more identityrelated stressors on 43.0% of days, the most frequent being "My identity interfered with my life" (12.6% of days), followed by "I worried that others would reject or not accept me due to my identity" (12.3%), "I actively concealed my identity from others" (11.7%), and "I saw or heard negative messages or stereotypes about my identity" (10.6%).

Participants reported having one or more positive identity-related experiences on 49.8% of days, the most frequently endorsed experiences being, "I had positive interactions with another person who shares my identity" (27.9% of days), "I saw or heard something positive about individuals with my identity (18.7%) and, "I felt that someone understood my experience as a person with my identity" (14.8%).

Additionally, participants frequently endorsed socially rewarding experiences not necessarily related to identity: "I felt close or connected to someone" was endorsed on 47.4% of days, and "I felt accepted or well-liked by someone" was endorsed on 27.9% of days.
On average, participants estimated that identity-related stress accounted for a relatively low percentage of overall daily stress (median = 8% of daily stress).
Qualitative feedback from Phases 1 and 2 informed several design choices for our measurement development, with broader implications for SGM mental health research.
First, participants reported stressors tied to current sociopolitical events, suggesting that measures need to comprehensively capture these experiences.

Notably, in the months prior to and during data collection for Phases 1 and 2 (which spanned April to June 2025), several significant federal and local sociopolitical events occurred and were directly cited by participants during qualitative interviews, including the start of President Trump's second term in January 2025, the Trump administration's executive order directing health agencies to restrict gender-affirming medical care to individuals younger than 19 (Protecting Children From Chemical and Surgical Mutilation, 2025), and the University of Virginia health system ceasing offering these services to new patients younger than 19 (Allard & Wu, 2025).

text.text: To address this feedback in our measure, we added "politics/current events" as a response option for the initial question in which participants indicate the overall domain of their first/second most stressful experience that day.

Additionally, we added the following response options to the select-all that apply questions characterizing daily identity-related stressors: 1) "I learned about laws/policies that would harm those with my identity," and 2) "I was directly impacted by laws/policies harmful to those with my identity."

The fact that the existing measures used to create the initial draft of the daily diary measure did not include such response options suggests that when studying phenomena tied to dynamic social and structural forces (e.g., changing cultural attitudes and policies), the way we measure these phenomena needs to change over time.
Second, participants emphasized that their most salient stressors each day were sometimes chronic, not necessarily starting and ending that day.

To address this feedback, we broadened the wording of certain questions to allow participants to answer with respect to chronic stressors (e.g., changing "Please think of the MOST stressful experience you had today" to "Please think of the experience that caused you the MOST stress today") and explicitly informed participants in the Phase 3 baseline visit that they could respond with respect to acute or chronic stressors: "… please think of the experience that caused the most stress that day.

So, it could be an experience that actually happened that day, but it could also be something that happened in the past, OR something that is more chronic and does not have a clear start and end time."

In general, experience sampling research about stress largely focuses on acute stressors (Weber et al., 2022), but the present study suggests measurement approaches that can additionally capture chronic stressors are warranted.
text.formatted: In general, experience sampling research about stress largely focuses on acute stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Weber et al., 2022)</ref>, but the present study suggests measurement approaches that can additionally capture chronic stressors are warranted.

text.text: Future research should investigate how best to capture how chronic stressors are experienced day-to-day among SGM emerging adults by comparing various strategies head-to-head (e.g., continuous scales vs. inventories vs. free response, etc.).
Finally, participants found the distinction between distal and proximal identity-related stressors to be confusing.

Initial versions of the daily diary measure specifically asked participants to describe that day's most and second most stressful distal stressors (phrased as the most stressful experience that day that "involved external events or other people").
This distinction was made in line with minority stress theory's separation of distal versus proximal stressors (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: This distinction was made in line with minority stress theory's separation of distal versus proximal stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: However, the qualitative interviews suggest this theoretical distinction may not fit with SGM emerging adults' phenomenological experience, and hence, that assessing one of these stressor types in isolation from the other may be difficult.

To address this feedback, for the current measure, we included both distal and proximal stressors in the same inventory, removing the need for participants to make this distinction, but allowing researchers to optionally separate these constructs after collecting the data.

The rates with which participants in Phase 3 completed the final version of the SGM-DEM support the feasibility of using the measure to capture SGM mental health-related experiences in the context of a multi-week data collection.
Specifically, participants completed an average of 84.4% of surveys and took an average of about seven minutes to complete each survey, suggesting the measure yields good compliance and is brief.
Descriptive statistics from Phase 3 revealed several findings that build on existing SGM mental health research.
First, identity-related stressors occurred often, but the most intense stressors were typically not identity-related.

That is, participants reported one or more identityrelated stressors on 43.0% of days, but identity-related stressors accounted for 15.4% of top two stressors, and a median participant-estimated 8% of total daily stress.

The finding that participants had an identity-related stressor on 43.0% of study days is consistent with a prior study of sexual minority adolescents (age 12 to 18 years), which found participants experienced an identity-related stressor on 40.2% of study days (Mereish et al., 2021; though notably their measure captured just distal stressors, whereas ours captured distal and proximal stressors).

text.text: Our study is the first to our knowledge to assess daily identity-related stress in the context of SGM emerging adults' overall daily life stress.

In line with prior work finding relationships, health, and work/school-related difficulties to be among the most salient stressors during emerging adulthood (Descary et al., 2026; Matud et al., 2023), our study found that similar stressor domains (academics/work/career development, social situation, family and home life, mental health) were most salient for SGM emerging adults (though notably both identity-related and non-identity-related stressors could be included in these domains).

text.text: The present study suggests identity-related stressors may account for a relatively small (though still substantial) proportion of overall daily stress among SGM emerging adults.

Second, proximal identity-related stressors were more common and more frequently a top two daily stressor relative to distal identity-related stressors (based on traditional proximal/distal categories).

For example, the proximal stressors, "I worried that others would reject or not accept me due to my identity" (capturing expectations of rejection), "I actively concealed my identity from others" (capturing identity concealment), "I felt negatively about my identity or people with my identity" (capturing internalized stigma), and "I felt like different identities I hold were in conflict" (capturing identity conflict) were all more common than the most frequently endorsed distal stressor, "I was misunderstood because of my identity" among top two stressors. 4 This result is aligned with a prior experience sampling study that found proximal identity-related stressors were more strongly associated with day-level negative mental health outcomes than distal stressors among Bisexual+ adults (Feinstein et al., 2022).

text.text: Additionally, this result appears consistent with the social safety perspective, a theoretical alternative to minority stress theory proposed by Diamond and Alley, which posits that SGM communities' elevated psychopathology risk is driven primarily by chronic safety-motivated threat vigilance (e.g., monitoring others for signs of potential rejection) during situations in which the level of social safety (i.e., reliable social connection, inclusion, and protection) is ambiguous or low (2022).

These findings support the notion that threat vigilance is a primary component of identity-related stress, and future work should assess if and how these experiences at the daily level may serve as a core pathway to mental health problems, consistent with the social safety perspective.

Third, results revealed that identity-related stressors were most typically related to SGM identities, but that stressors related to other identities (including combinations of identities) were common.

For instance, while participants most often reported that a top two stressor was related to a sexual minority identity followed by gender minority identity (59.6% and 29.5% of identityrelated/maybe-identity-related stressors, respectively), they also frequently reported that stressors were related to identity as a woman or man (22.9%), cognitive/psychological disability (12.7%), race (5.7%), and ethnicity (5.7%).
Negative intersectional experiences were also common.

For instance, participants reported that a stressor was related to two or more identities for 34.9% of identity-related or maybe-identity-related top two stressors, and the proximal stressor, "I felt like different identities I hold were in conflict," was endorsed for 12.3% of identity-related/maybeidentity-related top two stressors and 6.0% of days.

These results are consistent with prior work finding that SGM populations experience frequent stressors tied to the stigmatization of other marginalized identities they hold (e.g., racial/ethnic identities), as well as negative intersectional experiences (Jackson et al., 2020; Mereish et al., 2021).

text.text: This suggests that models of minority stress that account for such intersectional experiences (e.g., Rivas-Koehl et al., 2023) may more comprehensively capture the range of stressors faced by SGM emerging adults.
Further, results support the inclusion of identity conflict as a proximal stressor in models of SGM mental health, despite its absence from early models (Meyer, 2003).

text.text: Fourth, the most stressful daily experiences were largely offline (86.2% of top two stressors) versus online and involved other people about half the time.

That the top stressors were overwhelmingly offline is notable given emerging adults often form relationships and communicate with others through digital means (Hossain, 2026), and given recent research emphasizes the harms associated with social media use (Agyapong-Opoku et al., 2025).

text.text: It also suggests solitary stressors (e.g., perhaps academic-or work-related stressors) are just as salient.

Notably, the majority of participants in the Phase 3 sample were undergraduate college students, for whom prior research and the present study suggest that academics are the most frequent stressor (Pitt et al., 2018).

text.text: It could be that academics (which may presumably be coded by participants as offline and nonsocial) are driving these effects, and that findings would differ in samples of SGM emerging adults that have a smaller proportion of students.
Finally, results support the assertion that positive identity-related experiences are common, perhaps more so than identity-related stressors.
Specifically, in the present study, positive identity-related experiences occurred on 49.8% of days (vs.
43.0% of days for identityrelated stressors).

That positive identity-related experiences were so common among Phase 3 participants suggests they are core parts of SGM emerging adults' daily experiences and feasible to study in a daily diary format.

The similar prevalences of positive identity-related experiences and identity-related stressors in this sample (of mostly college students) is consistent with prior research finding SGM college students have mixed perceptions regarding whether their college environment is supportive, neutral, or hostile (Pitcher et al., 2018).

text.text: This study's findings should be considered in light of its limitations.
First, the research team decided on key aspects of the daily diary measure (e.g., overall content areas) prior to codesign, perhaps limiting the scope of recommendations the sample offered.

Second, while codesigning our daily diary measure with input from our target population is a strength, our study did not include a comprehensive psychometric evaluation of the measure (a weakness of experience sampling research in general: and minority stress experience sampling research in particular: Nicholas & Bresin, 2024).

text.text: Third, our sample differed slightly from the target population (SGM emerging adults) in some ways that may limit generalizability of the measure and study findings.

For example, our sample had a higher percentage of college students than SGM emerging adults as a whole, participants were all residents of the same city in the southeastern U.S. (which is relevant given prior research finding different levels of minority stress by geographic region; Pachankis et al., 2021), and certain racial/ethnic groups (e.g., Black SGM emerging adults) were not represented in Phases 1 and 2.

text.text: Further, while a broad measure of SGM mental health-related experiences may be useful for certain studies, researchers interested in narrowing in on experiences of SGM subcommunities (e.g., bi+ stress; Feinstein et al., 2022) may require more targeted measures.

text.text: Finally, given the present study provided tiered compensation (up to $80 or 4 research credits) based on survey completion, as well as occasional email/phone check-ins to support compliance-it is unclear how completion rates for the present measure may differ with different payment structures and compliance monitoring approaches.

The present study recruited SGM emerging adults to codesign a daily diary measure of SGM mental health-related experiences and deployed the final measure in a separate sample of SGM emerging adults for two weeks.

Qualitative data revealed several areas for improvement in the measure, including adding questions to explicitly capture stress tied to sociopolitical events, and adjusting language to also capture chronic stressors.

Quantitative data from participants who completed the final measure for two weeks revealed that non-identity-related stressors occurred more frequently than identity-related stressors, that proximal stressors were experienced more frequently than distal stressors, and that negative intersectional experiences and positive identityrelated experiences were both common.

Collectively, findings highlight the importance of involving participants with lived experience in all stages of the study design process when researching constructs linked to dynamic social and structural factors.
